en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Silk 15.
The Training Rule on Sitting Mats.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, I wish to dwell in seclusion for three months.
I am not to be approached by anyone except for one who brings me almsfood.
“Very well, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One, and no one at all approached the Blessed One except for the one who brought him almsfood.
Now at that time, a formal agreement had been made by the Saṅgha in Sāvatthī:
"Friends, the Blessed One wishes to remain in seclusion for three months.
No one should approach the Blessed One, except for a single person bringing almsfood."
“Whoever approaches the Blessed One must be made to confess a *pācittiya* offense.
Then the Venerable Upasena Vaṅgantaputta, together with his retinue, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Now it is the custom for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, to exchange greetings with visiting monks. Then the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Upasena Vaṅgantaputta:
“I hope it is bearable for you, Upasena; I hope you are getting by.
I hope you have come along this road without too much fatigue?
“It is bearable, Blessed One; I am getting by, Blessed One.”
“And we have come along this road, venerable sir, without fatigue.
Now at that time, a bhikkhu who was a co-resident pupil of the Venerable Upasena Vaṅgantaputta was sitting not far from the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One said to that bhikkhu:
“Are those rag-robes of yours agreeable, bhikkhu?”
“Venerable sir, rag-robes are not pleasing to me.
“But why, monk, are you a wearer of rag-robes?
“Venerable sir, my preceptor is a wearer of rag-robes; therefore, I too am a wearer of rag-robes.”
Then the Blessed One said to the Venerable Upasena Vaṅgantaputta: “Upasena, this assembly of yours is inspiring.
How, Upasena, do you discipline an assembly?
“Venerable sir, when someone asks me for full ordination, I say this to them:”
“Friend, I am indeed a forest-dweller, an alms-food eater, and a wearer of rag-robes.
If you too will become a forest-dweller, an alms-food eater, and a wearer of rag-robes, then I shall ordain you.
If he gives his assent to me, I ordain him; if he does not give his assent to me, I do not ordain him.
To whoever asks me for dependence, I say this:
“Friend, I am one who dwells in the forest, one who lives on almsfood, and one who wears rag-robes.
If you too will become one who dwells in the forest, one who lives on almsfood, and one who wears rag-robes, then I will give you dependence.”
“If he assents to me, I give him formal dependence; if he does not assent to me, I do not give him formal dependence.
It is in this way, Bhante, that I discipline the assembly.
“Excellent, excellent, Upasena! You discipline the assembly well, Upasena.”
“But do you know, Upasena, the agreement made by the Saṅgha at Sāvatthī? “I do not know it, Bhante.
“Upasena, an agreement has indeed been made by the Saṅgha at Sāvatthī:”
“Friends, the Blessed One wishes to dwell in seclusion for three months.
No one should approach the Blessed One, except for a single person bringing almsfood.
Whoever approaches the Blessed One must be made to confess an offense of expiation (pācittiya).”
“Venerable sir, the Saṅgha in Sāvatthī will be known by its own agreement:
‘We shall not prescribe what has not been prescribed, nor shall we abolish what has been prescribed;
having undertaken them, we shall conduct ourselves according to the training rules as they have been laid down.’”
“Excellent, excellent, Upasena!
That which has not been prescribed should not be prescribed, and that which has been prescribed should not be abolished;
one should undertake and practice according to the training rules as they have been laid down.”
“I allow, Upasena, those bhikkhus who are forest-dwellers, almsfood-eaters, and wearers of rag-robes to approach me for a visit as they please.
Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus were standing outside the gateway, thinking, “We shall cause the venerable Upasena Vaṅgantaputta to confess an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Then the venerable Upasena Vaṅgantaputta, together with his retinue, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and departed.
Then those bhikkhus said to the Venerable Upasena Vaṅgantaputta: "Do you know, friend Upasena, the agreement made by the Saṅgha at Sāvatthī?
"The Blessed One also asked me this, friends: 'But do you know, Upasena, the agreement made by the Saṅgha at Sāvatthī? 'I do not know, Bhante, the agreement made by the Saṅgha at Sāvatthī.
'Upasena, an agreement has indeed been made by the Saṅgha at Sāvatthī—'"
"Friends, the Blessed One wishes to remain in seclusion for three months.
No one should approach the Blessed One, except for a single person bringing almsfood.
Whoever approaches the Blessed One must confess an offense of expiation."
“Venerable sir, the Saṅgha in Sāvatthī will be known by its own agreement:
we shall not prescribe what has not been prescribed, nor shall we abolish what has been prescribed;
we shall undertake and abide by the training rules exactly as they have been prescribed.”
“Friends, the Blessed One has given permission: ‘Those monks who are forest-dwellers, alms-collectors, and wearers of rag-robes may come to see me as they please.
Then those monks thought: “The Venerable Upasena has spoken the truth:
‘What has not been laid down should not be laid down, and what has been laid down should not be abolished; one should undertake and practice the training rules exactly as they have been laid down.’”
The bhikkhus heard: “It seems the Blessed One has authorized it: ‘Those bhikkhus who are forest-dwellers, almsfood-eaters, and wearers of rag-robes may come to see me as they please.
Desiring a vision of the Blessed One, they discarded their rugs and undertook the practice of forest-dwelling, the practice of eating only almsfood, and the practice of wearing rag-robes.
Then, while wandering on a tour of the lodgings together with many bhikkhus, the Blessed One saw the rugs discarded here and there.
Having passed by, he addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, whose mats are these that have been discarded here and there?
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Thereupon, the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma regarding this cause and this occasion, addressed the bhikkhus:
“Therefore, monks, for ten reasons I shall lay down a training rule for the monks—
for the well-being of the Saṅgha, for the comfort of the Saṅgha … And thus,
monks, you should recite this training rule:”
“Now, when a monk is having a sitting mat made, he should take a Sugata-span from the edge of his old mat for the purpose of disfiguring it.
If a monk should have a new sitting mat made without taking a Sugata-span from the edge of his old mat, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture. Regarding the term *nisīdana*:
[it means a sitting mat.]
It is called "made from existing materials. What is called "spread" (santhata) is that which has been made by spreading [the materials], not woven.
"By one who causes to be made" means either doing it oneself or causing it to be done.
"Old cloth" (purāṇasaṇṭhataṃ) means:
Even if it has already been worn once or put on once,
a Sugata-span should be taken from the border to make it discolored; for the sake of making it firm,
one should cut it into a circle or a square and then sew it onto one part, or unravel it and sew it there.
If a monk, without taking a Sugata-span from the edge of an old sitting rug,
makes or has made a new sitting rug without taking a Sugata-span from the edge of the old sitting rug, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the act;
upon acquisition, it is an offense entailing relinquishment.
It should be relinquished to the Saṅgha, or to a group, or to an individual.
And thus, monks, should it be relinquished:
…pe…
“Venerable sir, this sitting mat of mine, which I have had made by adding a Sugata-span around the edge of my old mat without taking back the old material, is to be relinquished.
I relinquish it to the Saṅgha. …pe… “He should give it back” …pe…
"May he give it... ... [as before] ... "I give it to the Venerable One.
If one completes by oneself what was begun by oneself, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya pācittiya).
If one completes what was begun by oneself through others, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya pācittiya*).
If one completes what was begun by others through oneself, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If one completes what was begun by others through others, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If one makes it or causes it to be made for another purpose, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
There is no offense if one makes it by taking a Sugata-span from the border of an old rug.
If he does not obtain [enough], he makes it by taking a smaller amount;
if he does not obtain [any], he makes it without taking anything;
or he obtains what has been prepared by another and consumes it.
If one makes a canopy, or a floor-covering, or a screen-wall, or a mattress,
or a pillow— except for one who is insane or the first offender.
The fifth training rule concerning sitting mats is finished.
